before: Being held, not knowing a zeal for piety, he was not struck by the arrow of truth.

Therefore, he who sees one perishing and does not show zeal, as Paul says, 'Who is weak, and is not weak?' (1 Cor 9:27), is not a disciple of Paul. Let him compare the achievements of the Father, and he will find him agreeing with the apostolic voices: 'Who is weak, and is not weak?' 'Who is stumbled, and am I not burned?' Those thinking thus are brothers of the apostles.

For the righteous does not only lose heart in those things in which he sins, but also in those in which he sees others sinning, as David says: 'Despair has seized me because of sinners who have abandoned your law' (Ps 118:28). If anyone loses heart over the sins of others, he has a zeal for piety. For the righteous, when his own life is being corrected, weeps and mourns to erase his own sin; and then, having ceased from his own sin, he mourns the remaining sins of others, just as Paul [says]: 'Lest coming, I should mourn many of those who sinned before and did not repent' (2 Cor 13:10).

Paul mourns those who sinned and did not repent. Samuel mourns Saul, as God says: 'How long will you mourn over Saul?' (1 Sam 16:1). You see a soul perishing, and you do not mourn? If anyone sees a dead man being carried out, and does not weep, he is proven to be impure, hard, and beastly. If you see a soul being baptized in impiety, and being condemned to eternal death, and remaining in unfaithfulness, do you not weep, tell me, and mourn? And this is a pious soul?

Indeed, all other sins the one thinking well must mourn, except, however, when he sees a soul baptized in the impiety of Hellenism. Over such a soul one must not only mourn, but also be burned and consumed by zeal, so that he may become a disciple of Paul. For, he says, while Paul was rubbing [his way] in Athens, his spirit was consumed, seeing the city to be a sepulcher. Why then do the saints think these things, just as this wonderful one was a father avenging piety? For just as a king on earth, holding the inhabited world under him, has advocates assisting him in each court of the palace, so God has the faithful shepherds as avengers of piety. For many, frequently spreading [rumors] among the Greeks, say whatever...

Lest Christians hear those saying to them, 'Why do you blaspheme? Why are you impious?' and immediately they are dragged away; 'Behold the avengers of God; is God not able to avenge himself?' But He does not avenge himself (for He does not insult the divinity), but through faithful servants, the ignorant slaves, He lashes. Does God have need of avenging? Yes; not because He is weak, but so that He may open for you a door of zeal. For if He did everything by Himself, the way of life would be closed to the zealot.

Pharaoh never fought against God, though he was submerged in impiety; and nowhere was a lash brought upon him until Moses the faithful rose up. The many-godded error with the false priests and false prophets was not trimmed away, and nowhere was a plague from God, until Elijah the zealot rose up. The saints are, it is confessed, the avengers of God. Therefore also Paul says: 'We are ready to avenge all offense, when your obedience is fulfilled' (Rom 12:19).

Furthermore, the wonderful Deborah, having the weakness of a woman but prophesying the courage of virtue, about whom the Scripture says, 'And Deborah arose, a mother in Israel' (Judg 4:4), and she became a mother to the people through piety, and she flourished so much that she even says to the generals of war, regarding those around Barak: 'If you do not come to war with us, we are not going.' They did not boast of the woman's courage, but of the power of prophecy. Many went out as co-workers of God's counsel, and they cut down the foreign tribes.

That blessed Deborah, bringing the truth, says: 'Lord, those who love you, like the rising of the sun; but your enemies, like the glimmer of a lamp' (Judg 5:31). Lord, those who love you, like the rising of the sun; because the sun is never extinguished; but your enemies, like the glimmer of a lamp; for a lamp has light for a short time, and again it is extinguished. Then He praises the general who ministered to God's counsel, and after these things He commands the inhabitants of Majore to be cursed, because they did not go out to the help of the Lord.

Did God then need help? Yes. It is necessary for those helping in piety to be revealed. Thus also this wonderful father does not help God as if He were powerless, but having been led to this, he avenges piety, demonstrating through the body toward destruction, but [for] souls...

before: Concerning the blind from birth (formerly under the authorship of John Chrysostom): On zeal and piety, and concerning the one blind from birth. The Word of God is the source of light; for being full of light and shining forth, it illuminates and surrounds the minds of the faithful. For He himself shines from Himself and in Himself, and gives brightness to those enjoying Him; and He not only illuminates the mind of the faithful, but also grants the name of light.

For the Divine Scripture, regarding those who are companions of ignorance and live with unbelief, justly names them darkness, because they do not receive the torch of truth, so that they might be sons of light. Therefore the divine apostle Paul says: We are not sons of night, nor of darkness, but sons of light and of day (1 Thessalonians 5:5). And just as we are truly sons of light through the evangelical Word spoken through the mouth of God: I am the light of the world, says Christ; he who follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life (John 8:12). For that Word is light, which, if believed by us, prepares one to become a son of light. Therefore the Savior says: While you have the light, believe in the light, so that you may become sons of light (John 12:36).

Just as this sensible light is upon the bodies, so the spiritual Word of God is upon the souls; and just as darkness is in the night, so ignorance is in the wandering souls. Therefore also the blessed David writes concerning such things, saying: They did not know, nor did they understand; they wander in darkness (Psalm 95:11). Thus also God calls the assembly baptized in ignorance, and unwilling to be awakened toward the knowledge of the spiritual teaching, night, because of the ignorance living with it.

For when God was saying to the Jews through the prophet: I likened your mother to a night (Hosea 2:17); and interpreting what kind of night he means, like darkness, he added: My people were made like a people not having knowledge. Because of this, they did not know, nor did they understand; they wander in the night (Psalm 95:11).

But they are thus; but those having received the teaching of Christ, having received the light, such are made light. For our God is light; and his Word, who from himself being impassibly begotten before the ages, is called light; and the holy and consubstantial and life-giving Spirit, light. Light, and light, and light; but one light; and the soul having received the word, is named light.

But God is by nature a tri-hypostatic light, but we are by participation in him; and again our Lord Jesus Christ is light, concerning whom the evangelist John says: 'The true light was coming, which enlightens every man coming into the world' (John 1:9). But being light existing from unutterable light, and the law is sent through a light-bearing source, according to the prophet saying: 'Your law is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths' (Psalm 119:105).

Therefore the soul having received the truth, the luminous word, and it itself is made light, and it hears from Paul: 'For you were once darkness, but now light in the Lord' (1 Cor 6:9). And when the intellect receives the evangelical light, it is named light according to faith; and likewise also according to works. For 'let your light shine' (Matt 5:16), he says, 'before men, so that they may see your good works, and may glorify your Father who is in the heavens.' For it is necessary for the one having received the light of faith to come even into works of light.

And it is not only necessary for the soul of the believer to be light, but also according to works to shine before men; for this reason also the Savior says: 'Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works, and may glorify your Father who is in the heavens' (Matt 5:16). And behold the wonderful thing: for the light from God is simple, but it has diverse rays not by nature, but by activities; and the shining teaching of God is sent upon every believing soul, according to the thing said: 'And let the brightness of the Lord our God be upon us, so that by him our works may be directed' (Psalm 89:17).

before: Ours. There is one brightness, but coming to us it constitutes many brightnesses: the brightness of almsgiving, the brightness of temperance, the brightness of hospitality, the brightness of familial affection. Toward God there is one brightness; but this, being sent to us, constitutes diverse gleamings through diverse activities: to one, the brightness of prophecy; to another, the brightness of apostleship; to another, the brightness of martyrdom.

There, there is one brightness; but toward us, there are many, according to what has been said: 'With you is the beginning in the day of your power, in the brightnesses of your saints.' Why then does Paul enumerate, and say: 'Are not all apostles? Are not all prophets? Are not all teachers?' (1 Cor 12:29-30). Paul does not divide thus simply, but as he finds souls of fitness; he does not divide according to authority, but according to the confession of the faith; not that he gives according to his own will, nor according to his desire, but that his will is not unmeasured, but according to the gifts of the graces.

For just as the flowery and brightly-colored royal garment receives a solar ray and produces diverse gleamings, and as the beauty is of the dye, so it achieves such splendor; and just as by the present dye it is re-dyed and the beauty of the air is turned into gold, or into purple, or into green, or into some other of the colors, not by the ray being divided, but by the garment, the ray's effect being shaped by the light: in such ways the beauty of the Church always shines with blossoms, having a royal garment and being adorned with a heavenly and variegated array; as also the psalmist says: 'Daughters of kings in your honor; the queen stands at your right hand, arrayed in gold of various colors' (Ps 45:13).

How is she variegated? By the gifts of the Holy Spirit, according to the voice of Paul: 'God working through signs and wonders and various powers, and the distributions of the Holy Spirit' (1 Cor 12:4-6). But what shall I name the Church of Christ? A bride having been adorned, a queen having been beautified, a paradise tending, a garden flowing with fruitfulness, and if I should say anything else, I speak of less than its worth. Therefore the prophet Isaiah, taking up the voice of the Church from her own person, was saying: 'Let my soul rejoice' (Isa 61:10).

Upon the Lord; for he clothed me with a garment of salvation. And since he was in a pattern, and he was unable to express the whole beauty of the Church, he sets before him a distinction, saying: As a bride he has adorned me with beauty, and as a bridegroom he has placed upon me a crown, and as a land increasing its offspring, and as a garden of vegetables its seed. For the Church of the living God is a garden truly as if enclosed and a paradise; but I say paradise not according to that ancient one, but much higher than that. For there a serpent reigned, but here Christ reigns.

4. Do not pay attention to the reliability of places, but to the power of the reality. For neither is a paradise wonderful if it does not have a God-command being kept; nor are the lowly places insulted if they have God reigning the law. What is better? what is superior? a paradise, or a desert? And yet, because of the transgression, paradise did not benefit Adam; but because of endurance, the desert did not harm Job. Adam is disgraced in paradise because of disobedience, but Job is crowned in the desert because of endurance.

For nowhere does the reliability of places contribute if good judgment is not running together; and the heaven is higher than paradise, but the devil falls from there. The earth is deep, and the heaven is suspended; the devil falls from heaven having transgressed, according to: I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven (Luke 3:9); but the poor are raised from the earth, according to: He raises the poor from the earth, and lifts the needy from the desert (1 Samuel 2:8). Do you see how it is not the difference of places that grants us advantages, but everywhere faith, and endurance, and hope weave the crowns for the worthy?

Nothing is more solemn than a bedchamber, nothing is more naked than a theater; what did adultery in a bedchamber benefit the unruly Egypt? what harmed the first martyr Thecla, to practice nakedness in a theater? She did not sin by being naked, the holy one is not insulted, but is crowned. And she who is in the theater is crowned, but she who is in the bridal chamber is honored. What did the idols benefit, and the worship of non-existents? I say the greatness of temples; but what harmed the martyrs, the poverty of the tombs? Error was not shamed in greatness, and the things of the martyrs were raised in humility; thus the Church of the living God...

before: Driving toward power, for the arrows of the powerful are ineffective. And do not marvel if the shepherds of Christ and teachers of piety avenge the truth; but even if one is not a teacher, not having trusted in a teaching throne, but having simply received the word of Christ and being in the rank of a disciple, he ought to have zeal for God, and to render rewards to the benefactor in speaking freely, and to speak on behalf of the truth, and to contend against impiety, so that he may hear from the Holy Scripture: 'Child, contend for the truth, and the Lord God will fight for you.'

It is nothing to marvel at if the holy ones avenge piety. Often [God] is called something through leniency, as a good God, and the prophets do not forgive piety being struck by the leniency of God. God says through Moses: 'Say to Pharaoh, Let my people go;' (Exodus 5:1) but if you do not want, behold, I will send signs, and I will strike you. Moses struck [the word] upon the word, and understanding is given to the pious, and he says: Do not think that he has a people out of equality, and God has a people. And Having contended, let not the great goodness and leniency of God hinder him, and let him not think he is opposing God, having heard: 'Your people, and My people,' the proclamation refers. Thus says the Lord God of the Hebrews: 'Let my people go;' (Exodus 5:1) but if you do not want, behold, I will send signs, and I will strike you and your servants; so that you may know that the earth and its fullness belong to the Lord (Psalm 24:1).

the land heard the people and the people, and did not follow the word, but says, 'All the earth is the Lord's.' For even if God used leniency, this does not betray the masterly authority. For this reason also God spoke thus, so that the zeal of the pious might be stripped bare. But the faithful also always love to exceed the words of God; for the Savior says to the disciples: 'What do men say the Son of Man is?' (Mark 4:36) One of the disciples says...

of him: 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.' May the zeal of the Holy Spirit teach you also to be zealous, and to suffer for the sake of piety, and to contend the good struggle for the sake of righteousness.

For it is worthy, the imitating of good teachers, to be good disciples, as also Paul says: 'Become imitators of me, just as I also of Christ' (Matt 9:27). Do you wish to learn whether even the simple disciple, having the rank of a disciple, ought to have zeal for piety? Listen how Christ healed the one blind from birth; but rather let us hear from the beginning of the history. For after many things having been said to the evangelist, thus he began to say: 'As Jesus was passing by, he saw a man blind from birth' (John 9:1). And his disciples asked him, saying, and the following (John 9:2). And having spat, and having made clay, he anointed his eyes, and said to him: 'Go, wash in the pool of Siloam'; and having washed, he looked up (John 9:6-7). The Jews knew him, and they say: 'Is not this the one sitting for alms, being blind?' (John 9:8). Others were saying, 'Yes'; others, 'No', but 'he is like him' (John 9:9). He was saying, 'It is I' (John 9:9).

But the Pharisees and the rulers of the Jews, seeing that the wonder has many attracting to Christ, being bitten by the zeal of impiety, and being struck by the sting of the truth, call the once-blind man in. And it was to see an evil theater, of piety being avenged, and of evil judges judging, and of a great advocate contending, and of God rewarding and overseeing. They call the once-blind and having seen again, the children of the Jews, and they set him in the midst of the council, and say to him: 'Tell how you received sight, and who opened your eyes to you, and what he did to you?' (John 9:15). These things they said, not that they might know, but that by the form of the question they might instill fear. For often the form of the question becomes to the one asked a teacher to answer, or to be silent; as if someone were to say to someone...

God says through Moses: 'Say to Pharaoh, Let my people go;' (Exodus 5:1) but if you do not want, behold, I will send signs, and I will strike you. Moses struck [the word] upon the word, and understanding is given to the pious, and he says: Do not think that he has a people out of equality, and God has a people. And Having contended, let not the great goodness and leniency of God hinder him, and let him not think he is opposing God, having heard: 'Your people, and My people,' the proclamation refers. Thus says the Lord God of the Hebrews: 'Let my people go;' (Exodus 5:1) but if you do not want, behold, I will send signs, and I will strike you and your servants; so that you may know that the earth and its fullness belong to the Lord (Psalm 24:1).

the land heard the people and the people, and did not follow the word, but says, 'All the earth is the Lord's.' For even if God used leniency, this does not betray the masterly authority. For this reason also God spoke thus, so that the zeal of the pious might be stripped bare. But the faithful also always love to exceed the words of God; for the Savior says to the disciples: 'What do men say the Son of Man is?' (Matthew 16:13) One of the disciples says...

of him: 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.' May the zeal of the Holy Spirit teach you also to be zealous, and to suffer for the sake of piety, and to contend the good struggle for the sake of righteousness.

For it is worthy, the imitating of good teachers, to be good disciples, as also Paul says: 'Become imitators of me, just as I also of Christ' (1 Corinthians 11:1). Do you wish to learn whether even the simple disciple, having the rank of a disciple, ought to have zeal for piety? Listen how Christ healed the one blind from birth; but rather let us hear from the beginning of the history. For after many things having been said to the evangelist, thus he began to say: 'As Jesus was passing by, he saw a man blind from birth' (John 9:1). And his disciples asked him, saying, and the following (John 9:2). And having spat, and having made clay, he anointed his eyes, and said to him: 'Go, wash in the pool of Siloam'; and having washed, he looked up (John 9:6-7). The Jews knew him, and they say: 'Is not this the one sitting for alms, being blind?' (John 9:8). Others were saying, 'Yes'; others, 'No', but 'he is like him' (John 9:9). He was saying, 'It is I' (John 9:9).

But the Pharisees and the rulers of the Jews, seeing that the wonder has many attracting to Christ, being bitten by the zeal of impiety, and being struck by the sting of the truth, call the once-blind man in. And it was to see an evil theater, of piety being avenged, and of evil judges judging, and of a great advocate contending, and of God rewarding and overseeing. They call the once-blind and having seen again, the children of the Jews, and they set him in the midst of the council, and say to him: 'Tell how you received sight, and who opened your eyes to you, and what he did to you?' (John 9:15). These things they said, not that they might know, but that by the form of the question they might instill fear. For often the form of the question becomes to the one asked a teacher to answer, or to be silent; as if someone were to say to someone...

before: A paradise of luxury exists while living. In that paradise the serpent danced and deceived; in this paradise the Savior says: 'Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall ever harm you' (Luke 10:19).

In the paradise, the way of life was closed to Adam because of the transgression; and so that God might show that a virtuous soul is not hindered, those outside the paradise receive greater things than those in the paradise. Paradise is shut off from Adam, but Peter is trusted with the keys of heaven; Adam is cast out of paradise, but Paul is caught up to the third heaven; the tree of life is barred from Adam; for God said, it is said, 'Lest Adam touch the tree of life' (Genesis 3:22). There life is forbidden, and the tree of life was forbidden by the transgressor; here the wood of the cross was brought, and all who desire to reap life eternal.

In the paradise, after the transgression, Adam hides from God, being struck by his conscience; he is called by Him who seeks all things, and says: 'Adam, where are you?' (Genesis 3:9). For did you not know where you were? 'Adam, where are you?' Rebuking his lawlessness, He says, 'Where are you?' instead of, 'In what [state] are you?' Did the deception of the serpent not bring you equality with God? Did you see how you became naked? 'Where are you?' 'I heard your voice, and I was afraid and hid.' That one hides in paradise; the apostles say, 'We all, with unveiled faces, reflect the glory of the Lord, from glory to glory' (2 Corinthians 3:18).

Did you see boldness outside the paradise? Did you see shame inside the paradise? In the paradise, after the transgression, God clothed Adam in tunics of skin. Let us see what he put on. That one there put on a tunic; here, 'as many as were baptized into Christ, have put on Christ' (Galatians 4:4). Having been shut out from paradise, the Cherubim and the turning sword were blocking the way of paradise; and it was like a wall and a fortification to Adam, not allowing him to enter because of the misconduct in the paradise after the transgression. I am not speaking against the paradise, but that that God-befitting place did not benefit the one who, not having willed to live with a good intention, desired to turn back. And there was a wall of fire surrounding the paradise, and not allowing the transgressor to enter...

to show that it was not the fire that was an enemy to him, but the transgression which prevented Adam from entering the wall of fire; and Elijah snatched up a chariot of fire into heaven (2 Kings 2:11). The Church of God does not lie, saying: God clothed me with a garment of salvation (Ps 18:10), and as a bride he adorned me with beauty, as a land increasing its offspring, and as a great garden of truth. This great garden is the universal Church.

Christ reigns, and as a lawgiver he is believed, unless someone should be found in the Church suffering from a heretical wandering, under the teaching of serpents—I am speaking indeed of heretical wandering—and being cast out from here, like Adam from paradise. For just as there, he who was persuaded by the teaching of the serpent was exiled from paradise, so also in the Church those not obeying Paul, not being taught by Peter, but being persuaded by the teachings of serpents, are cast out from this paradise.

Whence is this evident? Paul says: For I am zealous for you with a zeal of God; for I have betrothed you to one man, to present a pure virgin to Christ (2 Cor 11:2). But I fear lest, just as the serpent deceived Eve (Gen 3:13), so your minds might be corrupted. But there is no place here for the teaching of the serpent, since the Great Shepherd crushes the head of the serpents with the staff of faith. For just as a shepherd, our wonderful Father, crushes the heads of the dragons with the evangelical faith and the hope toward Christ; and as an excellent gardener and keeper, he nurtures the plants of the Church, but uproots if there is any illicit seed or shoot; he delivers the disease of impiety, the Greek wandering, as thorns to the fire; but the heretical wandering he casts out like wild weeds, clothed with the zeal of God, which many do not recognize.

For some have become accustomed to sophistically arguing against the Church and the holy shepherds, just as also against this wonderful father; and many, in the form of leniency, introduce laziness, and they insult zeal, and they attempt to blunt the word of God which is at its peak. For one can find someone in the form of leniency saying: What do we have in common with the Greeks? Does he wish to be saved? Let him be saved. He who says these things has not yet been inflamed with the zeal of piety; he who sees [someone] perishing, and does not mourn that person's loss, and [his] own ruin.

So do they: How did you see? Who opened your eyes? But he, caring less for the threat, possessed more of the truth, and says: A certain man, called Jesus, having made clay, anointed my eyes and said to me: 'Go, wash in the Siloam' (John 9:6). And having gone, I washed, and I saw. He did not know the truth, but he recognized the benefit; he did not yet know the merit of the benefactor. A certain man, having made clay, anointed my eyes, and I see.

The Jews did not believe that he was blind and had seen, until his parents of the one who had seen were called. The diversion of malice into doubt brought away the truth. They call the parents of the blind man; malice by itself brings witnesses together. The parents of the blind man were called.

Again the same form of questioning: 'This is your son, whom you say was born blind? (John 9:25) How then does he see now?' They, having perceived the way of malice, that they are bringing threats, say to them: 'We know that this is our son; and that he was born blind we know; but how he sees now, or who opened his eyes, we do not know; he has age, ask him; he himself will speak about himself. And see the wisdom of God.'

So that they might not divert his voice, the one who had seen, as if he were a child, or as if he did not know how to speak, as in common courts, God caused him first to be shown in the age of law. 'He has age,' they say; 'ask him'; because immature advocates are needed, but those bringing maturity, they themselves become their own advocates.

His parents answered and said: 'This is our son, and that he was born blind we know.' The parents testified so that there would be no doubt that he was not blind. 'He has age, ask him; he himself will speak about himself.' They call him again, he says, a second time, and say to him: 'What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?' He, moreover, having clothed himself with the zeal of God, unfolds the question, and as if for those unworthy of an answer, not worthy of a word, but what does he say to them? 'I have already said to you, and...'

“You did not hear; why do you wish to hear me again? Do you not also wish to become his disciples?” (John 7:40). And he who has not yet heard Christ's teaching imitates it. For the Jews, having surrounded the Savior in Solomon's Colonnade during the festivals (John 10:23), said to him: “How long will you lift up our soul? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.” He says to them: “I said to you, and you did not hear; why do you wish to hear again?” And see the piety of the advocate.

Because he paid attention to the malice of the Jews, for they do everything and shape threats and fear to be cast upon him so that he might not confess himself teacher, he says to them: “I said to you already, and you did not hear; why do you wish to hear again? Do you not also wish to become his disciples?” By saying, “Do you not also?”, he showed that the “I am” is being confessed. Let every Christian coming from Hellenism have this voice. For when a Greek meets you, having an ancient habit of error, and says to you, “Become a Christian,” say to him, “Yes; do you not also wish to become?”

The goal, therefore, of the one who recovered both soul and body, was such: “I said to you already, and you did not hear; why do you wish to hear me again? Do you not also wish to become his disciples?” Instead of [saying], “Stay this far from turning to me,” for I also more eagerly expect you, having been changed, to confess Christ himself according to the truth.

Then what [was] against him from the Jews? They mocked him and said: “You are a disciple of that man, but we are disciples of Moses. We know that God spoke to Moses; but this one we do not know from where he is.” Consider the multitude of the objectors, and the power of one standing against them. And the advocate of the truth did not be silent again, but stood firm, saying, “For in this it is wonderful,” saying, that you do not know from where he is, and he opened my eyes (John 9:35). If this man were not from God, he would not have been able to do anything. He stands struggling, and God is the overseer and the judge; many are terrible against one strong man, an unbelieving cloud against a single drop of faith. From the age, he says, it was not heard that someone opened the eyes of one born blind (John 9:32). If this man were not from God, he would not have been able to do anything. Because you magnify yourselves, he says, in the teaching of Moses. He does not mention Moses at all, so that—
